lesson.title: A Sea of Shared Electrons
lesson.summary: Metallic bonds arise when metal atoms pool their valence electrons into a shared, mobile electron sea surrounding a lattice of positive ion cores, which explains why metals conduct electricity, bend without shattering, and shine.
lesson.body:
Metallic bonding is the third major category of chemical bond, and it looks quite different from ionic or covalent bonding because it does not involve just two atoms transferring or sharing electrons with each other. Metal atoms generally have low ionization energies and only a few valence electrons, which means those electrons are held loosely and are not strongly tied to any particular atom. When a large number of metal atoms come together, each one contributes its valence electrons to a shared, delocalized pool that spreads across the entire sample, while the remaining positively charged ion cores arrange themselves in an orderly, repeating lattice. The result is often described as a lattice of positive ions immersed in a sea of mobile electrons, and the attraction between those positive cores and the surrounding negative electron sea is what holds the metal together.

This delocalized picture directly explains several properties that set metals apart from ionic or covalently bonded materials. Because the valence electrons are not confined to any single bond, they are free to move throughout the metal in response to an electric field, which is why metals are excellent conductors of electricity, and free to absorb and reemit a wide range of light frequencies, which produces the reflective, lustrous appearance common to metals. Because the bonding is not directional the way a covalent bond is, and does not depend on ions sitting in one exact alignment the way an ionic crystal does, layers of metal ion cores can slide past one another under stress without breaking any specific bond, since the electron sea simply reshapes to keep binding the shifted ions together. That sliding is why metals are malleable, able to be hammered into sheets, and ductile, able to be drawn into wires, instead of shattering the way an ionic solid does when struck.

The strength of a metallic bond depends heavily on how many valence electrons each atom contributes to the shared sea and how strongly the resulting positive ion cores attract that electron sea, both of which connect back to periodic trends discussed earlier. Sodium, with only one valence electron per atom and a relatively large ionic radius once that electron is removed, has a fairly weak metallic bond and a low melting point of about 98 degrees Celsius. Magnesium, right next to it, contributes two valence electrons per atom to the shared sea and forms a smaller, more highly charged Mg2+ core, both of which strengthen the metallic bond considerably, giving magnesium a much higher melting point of about 650 degrees Celsius. This pattern, more valence electrons and smaller, more charged cores producing stronger metallic bonding, mirrors the same effective nuclear charge logic that explains ionization energy and electronegativity trends.

Metallic bonding sits conceptually between the other two categories rather than being a strange exception to them. Like ionic bonding, it involves an attraction between positively charged cores and a surrounding cloud of negative charge, like covalent bonding, that negative charge is shared rather than fully transferred to a specific neighboring atom. What makes it distinct is scale: instead of sharing being confined to a pair of atoms, or transfer being confined to a pair of ions, metallic bonding shares valence electrons across an essentially unlimited number of atoms at once, which is exactly why a piece of metal behaves as a single connected structure rather than as a collection of individual bonded units.
